paragraphs.context: For many years, I have admired Japan’s literature and art.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the writer wrote this book.
paragraphs.simple: The writer loves old Japanese books, poems and pictures. She wanted to live inside those pictures: ride a fishing boat, drink tea in a teahouse and see cherry flowers float down a river. Writing this book felt like visiting the world of her dreams.

background.note: Old Japanese pictures printed from carved wood blocks. Many show everyday life in old Edo (Tokyo).
The pink flowers of cherry trees. In Japan people love them and go out to see them every spring.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the tree house story began.
paragraphs.simple: A magic tree house appeared in the woods in Frog Creek. It can take Jack and Annie to any time and place. It belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot.

background.note: A magic librarian from the old King Arthur stories. The tree house belongs to her.
The castle and city of King Arthur in the old stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: After Jack and Annie traveled on many adventures for Morgan, Merlin the
paragraphs.simple: Later, Merlin the magician sent them on "Merlin Missions". Teddy and Kathleen, two young sorcerers, helped them find things to save Camelot.

background.note: Teddy is a young sorcerer, and Kathleen is a selkie (a "sea girl" who can become a seal). Both learn magic in Camelot.

paragraphs.context: On their next four Merlin Missions, Jack and Annie once again traveled
paragraphs.simple: They went to Venice, Baghdad, Paris and New York. Merlin saw that they used magic wisely, so he gave them the Wand of Dianthus. With it they can make their own magic. Now they wait for Merlin again.

background.note: A magic wand shaped like a unicorn's horn. Merlin gave it to Jack and Annie in book 36.

paragraphs.simple: Teddy says that last time they were in the countryside. This time they must go to the capital city.

paragraphs.context: “Are you guys coming with us?” asked Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks if Teddy and Kathleen will come with them.

paragraphs.context: “I am afraid not,” said Kathleen.
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen says no. They must help Morgan, because Merlin is ill and Morgan now does a lot of his work.

paragraphs.context: “You have the wand, do you not?” asked Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy asks if they have the wand.

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” said Jack. He reached into his backpack and took out the
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes the Wand of Dianthus out of his backpack. It is twisted like a unicorn's horn.

paragraphs.simple: Teddy says that the wand will help them make their own magic.

paragraphs.simple: Annie says Merlin told them the same thing.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says Merlin did not explain how to use it.

paragraphs.simple: Kathleen gives the second rule: first try as hard as you can without the wand. Do not use it too quickly.

paragraphs.simple: Teddy gives the third rule: the magic command must have exactly five words. Choose them carefully.

paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to hear the rules again.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, I’ve got it,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she remembers the rules. They must go fast to help Merlin.

paragraphs.context: Teddy and Kathleen held up their hands.

paragraphs.context: “And this book from Camelot’s library will bring you back home to
paragraphs.simple: Teddy gives them the Pennsylvania book. It will take them home after the mission, as on their first adventures.

paragraphs.context: “Good-bye,” said Annie. “Take good care of Merlin.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks them to look after Merlin well.

paragraphs.context: “We will try,” said Kathleen. She and Teddy raised their magic rings
paragraphs.simple: Teddy and Kathleen whisper to their rings and blow on them. They fade into the cool morning air and are gone.

paragraphs.context: Silence filled the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is silent.

paragraphs.context: Annie turned to Jack. “Ready?” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks Jack if he is ready.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. He pointed to the cover of the Japan book. “I
paragraphs.simple: Jack points at the cover of the Japan book and wishes to go there.

paragraphs.simple: The tree house starts to spin.

paragraphs.simple: It spins faster and faster.

paragraphs.simple: Then nothing moves.

paragraphs.simple: Everything is completely still. The magic has worked.

paragraphs.simple: Jack opens his eyes. Soft morning light comes in, and pink flowers are on a branch outside.

paragraphs.simple: The magic has given them new clothes: brown pants, brown silk robes with blue belts, white socks and straw shoes. Jack's backpack is now a cloth bag.

paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the robes look like bathrobes.

paragraphs.context: “I think they’re called kimonos,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks these robes are called kimonos.

background.note: A traditional Japanese robe with wide sleeves, tied with a wide belt (a sash).

paragraphs.simple: They look out the window to see where they have landed.

paragraphs.context: Below the tree house was a beautiful garden filled with cherry trees
paragraphs.simple: Below them is a garden with cherry trees, willow trees, a waterfall and a green pool.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened the Japan book and found a painting that looked like the garden.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a picture of the garden in the Japan book and reads aloud.

paragraphs.context: In the 1600s, the Imperial Garden surrounded the Imperial Palace in the
paragraphs.simple: In the 1600s the Imperial Garden was around the palace in Japan's capital city, Edo. Later, in the 1800s, Edo was renamed Tokyo.

background.note: The old name of Tokyo, the capital of Japan today. It was called Edo until 1868.
The palace in the middle of Edo (Tokyo). Today the emperor of Japan lives there.

paragraphs.context: “Tokyo?” said Annie. “I’ve always wanted to go to Tokyo!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie has always wanted to visit Tokyo.

paragraphs.context: “Me too,” said Jack. He read on:
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to go too. He keeps reading.

paragraphs.context: The late 1600s in Japan were years of peace and prosperity.
paragraphs.simple: In the late 1600s Japan was peaceful and rich, and art grew. But no foreigners could come in. People in Edo were often checked for passports.

background.note: From the 1630s to the 1850s, Japan kept almost all foreigners out, and Japanese people could not leave.

paragraphs.context: “What’s a passport exactly?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks what a passport is.

paragraphs.context: “It’s an official booklet that says who you are,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: A passport is an official little book that shows who you are and where you have traveled.

paragraphs.context: Anyone who did not have a passport was considered a spy and punished severely.
paragraphs.simple: A person with no passport was thought to be a spy and was punished very hard.

paragraphs.context: “Uh-oh,” said Annie. “We don’t have passports.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees the problem: they have no passports.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, that’s a problem,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agrees it is a problem.

paragraphs.context: “Hey! What if we use the Wand of Dianthus to make passports?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to make passports with the magic wand.

paragraphs.context: “Good idea!” said Jack. He peeked inside his bag. Good, the Wand
paragraphs.simple: Jack likes the idea and checks that the wand is in his bag.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, wait,” said Annie. “We can’t. Remember the rules. We can only
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers the first rule: the wand works only to help others, not themselves.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, right,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says OK. He remembers they can only use the wand to help others.

paragraphs.context: “And we have to try our hardest before we use the wand,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: They must also try their hardest before they use it.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says they have not tried anything yet.

paragraphs.simple: A bell rings, then they hear horses. They hide and look out. A line of people on foot and on horses is coming through the garden.

paragraphs.simple: A man rings a bell. Two men carry flags. Four men ride horses. Their heads are shaved except for knots of hair, and each has two swords.

paragraphs.context: At the very end of the procession rode a man in a
paragraphs.simple: At the end rides a man in a big purple robe and a purple hat, on a large black horse.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked at their research book again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a picture of the man in the book and reads the words under it.

paragraphs.simple: In the 1600s the army ruler, the shogun, lived in a huge palace in the middle of the Imperial Garden.

background.note: In old Japan, the shogun was the army leader who really ruled the country. The emperor had less power.

paragraphs.context: “That last guy is a shogun,” Jack whispered to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie that the last man is the shogun.

paragraphs.context: Often the shogun’s warriors traveled with him.
paragraphs.simple: The shogun's warriors often traveled with him. They were called samurai.

background.note: The warriors of old Japan. They carried two swords and followed strict rules.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” whispered Jack. “Those other guys are samurai!” He and Annie
paragraphs.simple: Jack is worried. On their first trip to Japan they only just got away from a samurai.

paragraphs.context: Samurai were excellent horsemen well trained in the arts of fighting.
paragraphs.simple: Samurai rode horses well and were trained to fight. Their rules were strict. They hid their feelings and could think very hard about one thing.

paragraphs.context: “They’re gone,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The procession has left.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window. The shogun and his samurai warriors had
paragraphs.simple: The shogun and the samurai go away down a shady road.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must leave the garden fast. If they stay, they will be caught.

paragraphs.context: “How do we get out?” asked Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks how to get out.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked in the Japan book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a map of Edo. They must cross a bridge on the east side of the garden into the city.

paragraphs.context: “The morning sun is over there,” said Annie, squinting into the sunlight.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees the morning sun, so that way is east. They will go that way.

paragraphs.context: “Good plan. Then we’ll be walking in the opposite direction of those
paragraphs.simple: Going east also takes them away from the samurai.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Annie. She started down the rope ladder.
paragraphs.simple: Annie climbs down the rope ladder.

paragraphs.context: “Be careful,” said Jack. “We don’t want anyone to see us sneaking
paragraphs.simple: Jack warns her that no one must see them in the garden.

paragraphs.context: Jack put the Japan book into his burlap bag and slung the
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the book in his bag. He almost falls on his long kimono, so he holds it up and climbs down carefully.

paragraphs.context: Jack joined Annie on a wide path.
paragraphs.simple: A dry wind blows cherry petals through the air. The willow branches move in the wind.

paragraphs.simple: They walk east, watching and listening for people. They pass flowers, rocks and a pond with swans.

paragraphs.simple: Four men walk toward them. One is older, with a straw hat, an old brown coat and a walking stick. The other three are samurai with swords.

paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that three of the men are samurai.

paragraphs.simple: They turn and run back down the lane.

paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie stop and turn to face the three samurai.

paragraphs.simple: A samurai holds up his sword and asks angrily if they are spies.

paragraphs.simple: Before Jack can answer, someone calls out two names: "Baku! Koto!"

paragraphs.simple: The man with the walking stick hurries over. He talks to Jack and Annie as if they are Baku and Koto, and asks why they did not wait at the bridge.

paragraphs.simple: A samurai asks the man if he knows Jack and Annie. He calls the man "Master".

paragraphs.simple: The man says they are his best students, Baku and Koto. He is helping them.

paragraphs.simple: The man says sorry that his friends frightened them.

paragraphs.simple: The samurai puts his sword away, says sorry and bows.

paragraphs.context: “Sure, no problem,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it is all right.

paragraphs.simple: The samurai thank the man very politely, calling him "Most Honored Master". They bow deeply and leave.

paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders why the samurai speak to this small man with such respect.

paragraphs.simple: The man's eyes shine with fun. He says they are safe now.

paragraphs.context: “Thanks,” said Annie. “But I’m afraid we’re not Baku and Koto.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thanks him but says they are not really Baku and Koto.

paragraphs.context: “No, you are not,” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: The man knows. He also thinks they are not spies.

paragraphs.context: “I did not think so,” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: He did not think they were spies, so he helped them.

paragraphs.context: “You are most welcome,” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: The man politely asks who they really are and how they got into the Imperial Garden.

paragraphs.context: “Our names are Jack and Annie,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gives their names but stops. He cannot easily explain Teddy and Kathleen, Merlin's sadness and Morgan's book.

paragraphs.context: “We came here to search for a secret of happiness,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they are looking for a secret of happiness.

paragraphs.simple: The man says everyone looks for that. But no foreigners may come into Japan, so without passports they could be caught and punished.

paragraphs.simple: Annie asks for advice.

paragraphs.simple: The man says they can travel with him today and keep being his students.

paragraphs.simple: He tells them to live in harmony with what is around them: watch the people of Edo and do the same. Then the samurai will not notice them.

paragraphs.simple: Annie understands.

paragraphs.simple: Jack asks why the samurai called him "Most Honored Master".

paragraphs.simple: Basho says he is their teacher.

paragraphs.simple: Jack asks what he teaches.

paragraphs.simple: Basho says the samurai learned to listen to a cricket in a pile of wood and to think like a frog. (He teaches poetry, but Jack does not know that yet.)

paragraphs.simple: Basho asks if they can ride down the river in the boat.

paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie sit on the boat next to the baskets.

paragraphs.simple: People have rebuilt Edo, and it is now more beautiful than before. Many new samurai castles stand by the river.

paragraphs.context: The poet Basho was born in Japan in 1644.
paragraphs.simple: Basho was born in 1644. His family wanted him to be a samurai, but he chose to write poetry.

paragraphs.context: Basho was poor and unknown for many years.
paragraphs.simple: Basho was poor at first, but later he became famous. His fans built him a house and a student gave him a banana tree. In 1682 a fire burned the house. Edo had many fires because its buildings were wood.

background.note: The Great Fire of Meireki in 1657 burned most of Edo. It is the fire Basho talks about in the story.

paragraphs.context: A new house was built for Basho, but he did not live
paragraphs.simple: He got a new house but soon began traveling around Japan. He wrote a famous travel book with poems, The Narrow Road to the Deep North.

background.term: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
background.note: Basho's most famous book (1694), about a long walk through northern Japan. It mixes travel writing and haiku.

paragraphs.context: The form of poetry that Basho is famous for is called haiku
paragraphs.simple: Basho is famous for haiku, the shortest kind of Japanese poem. It uses plain words about everyday things, but it can help you see life in a fresh way.

background.note: A haiku has three lines. In Japanese the lines have 5, 7 and 5 sounds.
